title: UK complicity
lede: Public contracts, a privatised monopoly, arms licensing and who gets to speak when the law is tested.
intro: A category that gathers existing, sourced pages on one theme: when official oversight is late, narrow or left to other jurisdictions, who is watching? Each chapter points to a page that carries the evidence and the caveats. This hub does not allege that any named person has broken the law. Questions stay questions.

chapters.title: Palantir, a former Met commissioner and Lord Mandelson
chapters.summary: The Bureau of Investigative Journalism reported that Dame Cressida Dick, former Metropolitan Police commissioner, has been a paid Palantir adviser since September 2025; she has denied lobbying. Official records also show that Lord Peter Mandelson, co-founder of Global Counsel, was UK ambassador to the United States when the Prime Minister visited Palantir’s Washington offices on 27 February 2025, in a quarter when the statutory lobbyist register listed Global Counsel Ltd as a lobbyist for Palantir. He was withdrawn as ambassador on 11 September 2025 for reasons the government stated in relation to Jeffrey Epstein, not Palantir. The linked page sets out those sources and leaves the conflict-of-interest questions as questions.

chapters.title: Thames Water: how a stable monopoly reached about 86% gearing
chapters.summary: A privatised water monopoly, with customers who cannot switch network, recorded net debt of £19.8 billion and gearing of about 86% of regulated value in 2025/26. The existing investigation follows the debt, shareholder distributions, the pollution record and the question the page itself poses: where were the regulators?

chapters.title: Gaza: official findings and people’s tribunals
chapters.summary: A fuller Gaza tribunal investigation on this site is forthcoming. In the meantime the watchdogs page records the UK government’s own 2 September 2024 finding of a “clear risk” that certain arms exports to Israel might be used in serious violations of international humanitarian law, the suspension of around 30 of approximately 350 licences, and the F-35 carve-out. Two concluded people’s tribunals, already documented here, are linked below: the international Gaza Tribunal, and the UK inquiry into British complicity.

chapters.title: Who gets to speak at the World Court?
chapters.summary: Before the International Court of Justice, only states may be parties in contentious cases. The Statute requires each party to be represented by an agent and allows counsel or advocates, but neither the Statute nor the Rules of Court say who a state may appoint or how the appointment is made: that is left to each state’s domestic arrangements. The Court regulates the agent’s role, not the choice of person. It also has no compulsory ethics code for those who appear.
